I've just never really experienced them in isolation like that.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances where you were able to control your impulsivity and restlessness, but still struggled significantly with inattention and disorganization, or has it always been that when one set of symptoms is manageable, the other is as well?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure because it's really hard to separate the two. The trouble with applications and the constant interrupting both happen so often that I've never really tried to compare their frequency. My tendency to jump into conversations and my trouble focusing feel like they're completely tangled up together. I can't really think of any times when one of them happens without the other.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a situation where you felt extremely restless or had a strong urge to move, but you were still able to focus and complete a task without interrupting others or making impulsive decisions?\n\nPatient: I can't recall a single time where I was feeling that restless but still managed to stay focused and finish what I was doing. I either have to get up and walk away, or I just end up getting totally distracted and never finish the task.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with restlessness and impulsivity are more prominent and problematic for you in most situations, or is it really the combination of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms that equally affects your daily functioning and causes you distress?\n\nPatient: It’s definitely the combination of both that causes me the most distress. While the attention issues and disorganization directly stop me from finishing my applications and certifications, the restlessness and constant need to move make it almost impossible to sit still and actually try to focus in the first place. It really is a double whammy where both sides of it constantly mess up my daily life.\n\nDoctor: Looking back at your experiences, do you feel that there have been times when either your inattention or your hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms were significantly more severe or prominent than the other, or have they generally been equally problematic for you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure and I haven't really thought about which one is worse. Both the attention issues and the physical restlessness have been causing me a lot of trouble, and they honestly feel equally hard to handle.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any period in your life, such as during childhood or in different living situations, where one set of symptoms, either the inattention or the hyperactivity-impulsivity, was clearly more problematic than the other, and if so, what was different about that time?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure and I haven't ever thought about one being worse than the other. As far as I can remember, both the attention problems and the restlessness have always gone hand-in-hand and caused trouble for me together since childhood. They've just always been mixed together for as long as I can recall.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific situations or environments where you feel that one set of symptoms, either your inattention or your hyperactivity and impulsivity, becomes more manageable or less bothersome than the other?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way before. Both the attention issues and the restlessness seem to cause me trouble in almost every situation, so I don't think one is ever clearly easier to manage than the other.\n\nDoctor: When you're in a situation where you can move around freely, like working on cars, do you find that your attention and focus improve, or do you still struggle with completing tasks and following through on your interests?\n\nPatient: Even when I'm working hands-on with cars, which I love, I still struggle to stay focused. For me, the attention issues and the restlessness usually feel completely tangled together and happen at the exact same time. I've just never really experienced them in isolation like that.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances where you were able to control your impulsivity and restlessness, but still struggled significantly with inattention and disorganization, or has it always been that when one set of symptoms is manageable, the other is as well?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure because it's really hard to separate the two. I usually feel like both the restlessness and the focus issues are happening at the exact same time, and they are always equally hard to manage.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any daily activities or tasks where you are able to control your impulsivity and restlessness without struggling with inattention, such as hobbies or routine chores?\n\nPatient: I honestly can't think of any activities or chores where I can successfully control these symptoms. Even with things I really enjoy, like working on cars, or just basic household chores, I still find myself getting distracted, switching between tasks, or feeling constantly restless. It just seems to affect everything I try to do.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often you experience significant problems with inattention, such as not being able to finish tasks, on days when you do not have significant restlessness or impulsivity, and vice versa?\n\nPatient: It's really hard to separate them because I feel like both the attention issues and the restlessness happen pretty much every day together. I don't really have days where I only experience one or the other. They both just seem to affect me at the same time, every single day.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you were able to focus and complete a task without any issues, but still exhibited impulsive behaviors or restlessness, such as interrupting others or fidgeting?\n\nPatient: I can't really think of a situation where I could focus perfectly and finish a task without any issues while still being restless or impulsive. Usually, when I am feeling restless, fidgety, or impulsive, my focus is also completely off and I end up getting distracted or leaving the task unfinished.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a situation where you experienced significant inattention, such as difficulty following instructions or completing tasks, without also feeling restless or impulsive, and if so, how did you manage to stay focused?\n\nPatient: I don't really have a successful way of managing to stay focused, and it's hard to separate the inattention from my restlessness. Even when I try to sit still and focus on a task like a job application, my mind drifts and I quickly start feeling that build-up of restless energy and the urge to move.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity are equally problematic and intertwined in all situations, or are there specific contexts where one set of symptoms clearly dominates over the other?\n\nPatient: Actually, different symptoms definitely dominate depending on what I'm trying to do. When I'm doing desk work like filling out job applications, studying, or organizing paperwork, the inattention, getting sidetracked, and feeling overwhelmed are what take over. But when I have to sit still or wait—like in waiting rooms, lines at the bank, or during family discussions—the restlessness, fidgeting, and urge to interrupt completely dominate.\n\nDoctor: When you're in situations that require a lot of physical activity, like working on cars, do you find that your impulsivity, such as interrupting others, is still a significant problem, or is it more manageable compared to when you're in sedentary situations?"
